walkthroughs.body_html: The Dorset Jurassic Coast (185 km, UNESCO World Heritage since 2001) exhibits 185 million years of rock history. East-west concordant at Lulworth Cove (Portland limestone, Purbeck beds, Wealden clays, Chalk) creates a cove where the sea breached the resistant limestone. Further east, the discordant coast at Studland Bay alternates resistant chalk headlands (Old Harry Rocks) with softer clay bays. Recession rates vary from ~1 cm/yr (chalk) to ~1 m/yr (clay).

The Norfolk Sandlings and Holderness coast comprise unconsolidated glacial till (boulder clay deposited during the Devensian). Cliffs at Happisburgh retreat at ~6 m/yr, among the fastest in Europe. Sediment from cliff erosion feeds the Norfolk sediment cell, building spits at Blakeney Point and Scolt Head Island via longshore drift driven by north-easterly waves. Loss includes 35 properties at Happisburgh since 1990.

Key contrasts: energy regime (Dorset: high-energy Atlantic swell; Norfolk: moderate North Sea fetch but storm surges), process dominance (Dorset: marine erosion + sub-aerial weathering; Norfolk: wave erosion + slumping of saturated till), landforms (Dorset: stacks, arches, coves; Norfolk: spits, bars, retreating cliffs), and management (Dorset: limited intervention; Norfolk: extensive defences and Shoreline Management Plans considering managed realignment).

mcqs.q: Why do some rivers form deltas and others form estuaries?
options: Deltas form where rivers deposit sediment faster than the sea can remove it (calm seas, heavy load); estuaries form where tidal energy removes sediment (strong tides).
Deltas form in cold climates and estuaries in warm climates.
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.
Deltas form on big rivers and estuaries on small ones.
